**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Recommendation on AI hardware capacity for the next two quarters

**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past month we've been asked repeatedly whether the right response to our growing inference workload is to purchase additional local GPU capacity or to invest in squeezing more out of the hardware we already own. This memo lays out my thinking ahead of Thursday's decision. The short version: I believe we should spend the next quarter aggressively improving utilisation of our existing fleet, with a pre-approved but not yet exercised option to purchase two additional accelerators at the end of that period if utilisation gains fall short of what the workload demands.

Let me start with the economics, because they frame everything else. Our current fleet represents a sunk cost of roughly £180,000, and our monitoring suggests the GPUs sit idle or underloaded for something like sixty per cent of peak-hour capacity. Buying more hardware at this utilisation rate would mean paying twice for the same headroom. A new accelerator costs not just its purchase price but power, cooling, rack space, and — less visibly — the engineering time to integrate, monitor, and maintain it. Every hour we spend provisioning new machines is an hour not spent on the product work that actually generates revenue. That opportunity cost is real, and it cuts in favour of the cheaper, faster option first.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and I want to take it seriously rather than wave it away. Our p99 inference latency has crept upward as batch queues have lengthened, and two of our customer-facing features are now brushing against the threshold where users notice. If utilisation work means batching more aggressively or introducing queueing, we risk trading throughput for tail latency, which would be a poor bargain for interactive workloads. My view is that this risk is manageable: a meaningful share of our current waste comes not from deliberate batching trade-offs but from scheduling inefficiency, models pinned to GPUs that are mostly idle, and batch sizes set once and never revisited. Fixing those things should improve latency and throughput together, at least up to a point. But I want to be honest that the point at which the trade-off turns sour is not something we can know precisely in advance.

Reliability considerations point in the same direction, with a wrinkle. A denser, better-scheduled fleet is easier to reason about than a sprawling one, and consolidation reduces the surface area for silent failures. However, higher utilisation also means less slack. Today, when a GPU fails, we absorb the load elsewhere and users barely notice. At eighty per cent utilisation, the same failure becomes a visible incident. Any utilisation push must therefore be paired with a concrete failover plan and, ideally, one machine's worth of deliberate reserve capacity. If we cannot maintain that reserve, the reliability argument starts favouring a purchase.

The reversibility question is where the decision becomes clearer. Utilisation improvements are almost entirely reversible and cheap to attempt: retuning schedulers, consolidating models, and improving autoscaling can be unwound in days if they cause problems. Hardware purchases are not reversible in any practical sense. Once bought, accelerators depreciate whether or not we need them, and reselling specialised hardware recovers only a fraction of its cost. When one option is cheap, fast, and reversible, and the other is expensive, slow, and sticky, the rational sequence is to exhaust the first before committing to the second — provided the first can plausibly deliver what we need, which I believe it can for at least the next two quarters of forecast growth.

So, the recommendation: fund a focused four-week utilisation effort with a measurable target — p99 latency held flat or better while absorbing projected Q3 load at no more than seventy-five per cent peak utilisation. If we hit that target, we defer purchase and revisit in the autumn with better data. If we miss it, the two-accelerator purchase proceeds without further debate, because we will have demonstrated the ceiling of what we own.

The main uncertainty worth naming is demand itself. Our growth forecast has been wrong in both directions this year. If a new customer lands in the next six weeks, all of this analysis compresses and we should buy immediately. I'd rather make that call with the utilisation work done than without it.

Happy to discuss Thursday.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Recommendation on our inference capacity decision
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past month we've been circling a question that deserves a firmer answer than the one we've been giving each other in hallway conversations: do we purchase additional local hardware to serve our inference workloads, or do we invest the next quarter in squeezing more out of the machines we already own? I want to lay out my thinking here, not because I'm certain, but because the cost of continuing to defer this decision is quietly growing.

Let me start with the honest picture of where we stand. Our current fleet runs at roughly 40–45% average utilisation, but that average hides the real problem: utilisation is spiky. During business hours, and especially during batch evaluation runs, we saturate our GPUs and queue times climb into territory that our internal users notice and complain about. Overnight and on weekends, the same hardware sits nearly idle. The bottleneck is not raw capacity in aggregate; it is capacity at the moment it's needed. That distinction matters enormously for the decision in front of us, because buying more hardware solves the peak problem only by making the trough problem worse.

The financial case for buying is straightforward on the surface. Another node would cost us capital up front, plus power, cooling, and rack space, and — the number we habitually underestimate — the engineering time to integrate, monitor, and maintain it. But the deeper cost is opportunity cost. Every dollar and every engineer-hour we sink into expanding the fleet is a dollar and an hour not spent on the product work that actually justifies our existence. And hardware depreciates. The accelerators we'd buy today will be outclassed within eighteen months, which means we'd be locking in today's assumptions about model sizes and traffic patterns at the exact moment when both are least predictable.

The case for improving utilisation is weaker on paper and stronger in practice. Scheduling improvements, better batching, quantisation where quality permits, and moving our batch evaluation jobs into off-peak windows are all reversible, low-capital interventions. If we try them and they fail, we've lost a quarter of engineering time and learned something valuable. If we buy hardware and the demand forecast was wrong, we've lost a great deal more, and unwinding it is slow and painful — you can't easily return a rack of GPUs, and reselling them means eating the depreciation. Reversibility is worth real money, and in this comparison it sits almost entirely on one side of the ledger.

Latency and reliability deserve their own mention, because they're the strongest arguments for buying. Our interactive workloads do occasionally queue behind batch jobs, and a dedicated node would eliminate that contention entirely, giving us cleaner tail latencies and a simpler failure story — one machine's problems wouldn't cascade into everyone's. I take that seriously. But I don't think we've yet earned that conclusion. Most of our latency incidents in the past two quarters traced back to scheduling misconfigurations and a batch job that cheerfully monopolises memory, not to genuine capacity exhaustion. Fixing those is cheaper than buying our way out of them, and if we fix them and latency is still bad, we'll then be buying with evidence rather than with anxiety.

So my recommendation is this: spend the next quarter on utilisation work, with a specific and measurable goal. If, after implementing proper scheduling isolation, dynamic batching, and off-peak migration of batch work, our p95 queue times during business hours still exceed our agreed threshold, we commit to the hardware purchase with a clear budget line already scoped. That gives us a decision gate rather than an open-ended deferral, which I know is the worry some of you have — that "improve utilisation first" becomes a way of never deciding. It shouldn't be. The utilisation work has value even if we buy later, because whatever we buy, we'll run it better with these improvements in place.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Our demand forecast is genuinely fuzzy — the new internal tooling could double interactive traffic next quarter, or plateau. If the former happens, the buy case strengthens quickly, and we should revisit this memo rather than cling to it. The point of writing this down is to make our reasoning inspectable, not to make it permanent.

Please come to Thursday with objections. In particular, I'd like the reliability folks to pressure-test my claim that our incidents are scheduling-driven, and finance to sanity-check the capital figures I've been using informally.

— Infrastructure Lead

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Recommendation on our next capacity decision
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past month we've hit GPU saturation on our inference cluster three times, and each incident has reignited the same debate: do we purchase additional hardware, or do we invest in raising utilisation of the machines we already own? I want to lay out my thinking before we meet, because I believe the framing we choose matters as much as the decision itself.

Let me start with the case that initially seems obvious. Our peak-hour utilisation sits around 85 percent, which sounds like a crisis. But averages tell a different story: across a full day, our fleet idles at roughly 40 percent. That gap between peak and average is the single most important number in this discussion. It tells us that our problem is not fundamentally a capacity problem — it is a scheduling and elasticity problem. We have built workloads that all want the hardware at the same time of day, and we are paying for idle silicon the rest of the time. Buying more GPUs would solve the peak problem, but it would also deepen the trough problem, and the trough is where our money quietly leaks away.

The cost arithmetic reinforces this. A new node carries not just its purchase price but power, cooling, rack space, and — the cost we habitually underestimate — the engineering time to integrate, monitor, and maintain it. Against that, the utilisation work we've scoped involves batching improvements, better request routing, a modest amount of model quantisation, and moving our batch analytics jobs into the overnight trough. None of it is glamorous, and some of it carries real risk: aggressive batching can add tens of milliseconds of latency, and quantisation, if done carelessly, degrades output quality in ways our users will notice before our dashboards do. But the latency cost is bounded and measurable, whereas the cost of new hardware is permanent and compounding.

Latency deserves its own paragraph, because it is where the two options genuinely diverge. Our interactive workloads have a p99 target we are already brushing against at peak. More hardware would buy headroom immediately and with near certainty. Utilisation improvements buy headroom too, but indirectly and with more uncertainty — better batching helps throughput first and latency only sometimes. If our latency targets were already failing, I would say buy now and optimise later. They are not. We are close to the edge, not over it, and that distinction should govern our sequencing.

Reliability cuts both ways. A larger fleet gives us more redundancy; losing one node among twelve hurts less than losing one among six. But our recent incidents were not hardware failures — they were demand spikes, and a second cluster does nothing to smooth demand. Meanwhile, the utilisation work includes better load-shedding and queueing behaviour, which directly improves how gracefully we degrade under stress. I would rather have a system that bends than a bigger system that snaps.

Then there is opportunity cost, which is the argument I find most persuasive. The engineering time for the utilisation project is roughly six weeks of two engineers. The same effort spent standing up new hardware would produce capacity, yes, but no lasting improvement in how we use any hardware we will ever own. Utilisation work is knowledge that compounds; hardware depreciates. If we later do buy more capacity — and we may — we will want the scheduling and batching discipline in place regardless, because it makes every future dollar of hardware go further.

Finally, reversibility. Hardware is a one-way door. Once purchased, it sits on our balance sheet and in our rack, and the decision to buy it cannot be unmade, only amortised. The utilisation work is a series of small, individually reversible experiments: we can dial batching depth back, revert a routing change, restore full-precision models. In an environment where our traffic patterns are still shifting as the product evolves, I place real value on keeping our options open for another two quarters.

So my recommendation is this: commit to the utilisation work now, with a hard checkpoint in eight weeks. If peak utilisation has not come down below 70 percent, or if p99 latency has degraded beyond our target, we proceed with a hardware purchase at that point, informed by what we've learned. I want to be honest about the uncertainty here — our traffic forecasts have been wrong twice this year, and if growth accelerates, the buy decision may arrive sooner than this plan assumes. That is acceptable. What I want to avoid is buying hardware out of peak-hour panic and discovering six months later that we purchased a permanent cost to solve a temporary shape problem.

Please come to Thursday with objections, especially from those closest to the latency numbers.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Hardware investment decision for the next two quarters
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past month we've hit capacity ceilings on our local inference cluster three times, and each incident has restarted the same debate: do we buy more hardware, or do we get smarter about the hardware we already own? I want to lay out my thinking before we meet, because I don't think this is really a binary choice, and I'd rather we argue about the right framing than the wrong one.

Let's start with the case for buying. Our utilisation numbers look healthy on paper, but they hide an uncomfortable truth: our peak demand is spiky in a way that our current scheduling can't smooth out. When the evaluation pipeline, the internal copilot, and the customer-facing batch jobs all land at once, we queue, and queuing means latency that our engineers feel directly. That latency has a real cost, even if it never shows up on an invoice. An engineer who waits forty minutes for an experiment result doesn't just lose forty minutes; they lose context, they context-switch, and the experiment they were excited about often doesn't get run at all. If we're honest, some of our slowdown in iteration speed over the last quarter is probably attributable to this, though I'll admit the causal evidence is anecdotal rather than measured.

The case against buying, however, is stronger than it first appears. New hardware is expensive not just in purchase price but in the opportunity cost of the engineering time to rack, configure, and integrate it — time we'd otherwise spend on product work. More importantly, it's a largely irreversible commitment. GPUs depreciate fast, our demand curve is uncertain, and if the mix of workloads shifts toward API-based models or smaller quantised deployments, we'd be holding capacity we can't easily resell at anything close to what we paid. Reversibility matters. Buying hardware is a bet on our current workload profile staying stable for at least eighteen months, and I'm not confident enough in that forecast to make the bet at full size.

Which brings me to the alternative. Our utilisation during business hours is high, but overnight and weekend utilisation is embarrassingly low — batch jobs that could run at 2am are competing with interactive workloads at 2pm because we never built the scheduling discipline to separate them. A serious effort here would mean priority queues, better bin-packing of heterogeneous jobs, aggressive checkpointing so preemptible work doesn't lose progress, and possibly moving our least latency-sensitive workloads to spot API capacity during peaks. None of this is glamorous, and all of it takes engineering time that we'd otherwise spend shipping features. That's the honest trade-off: improving utilisation isn't free, it just spends time instead of capital, and time is often our scarcer resource.

So where does that leave us? My recommendation is that we spend the next six weeks on utilisation work before committing to any purchase, with one carve-out: if we can identify a specific, recurring, measured bottleneck that scheduling genuinely cannot solve — for instance, interactive demand that structurally exceeds our interactive-capable capacity even with perfect packing — we should buy a small increment then, rather than a large one now. A modest purchase made with good utilisation data is reversible in a way a large speculative one isn't; we can always add more, but unwinding an overbuy is painful.

I want to be clear about the uncertainty here. My utilisation figures come from coarse monitoring, and it's possible that what looks like a scheduling problem is actually a hard capacity wall that no amount of cleverness will fix. If the six-week effort yields less than a 20% effective capacity improvement, that itself is valuable information, and it should trigger the purchase conversation with much better evidence than we have today. Conversely, if we get the improvements I suspect are available, we may find that the pressure to buy was partly an artifact of poor visibility rather than genuine scarcity.

The deeper principle I'd like us to adopt: exhaust cheap reversibility before expensive irreversibility. Scheduling improvements can be undone, tuned, or abandoned at low cost. Hardware cannot. Let's spend Thursday debating whether my utilisation estimates are realistic, and if anyone has data suggesting they're not, I'd genuinely like to see it before we commit either way.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI compute capacity for the next two quarters

**Summary**

We are at the point where demand for local inference and fine-tuning is brushing against the ceiling of our current hardware. The instinctive response — buy more GPUs — deserves scrutiny, because our own telemetry suggests we are not yet constrained by capacity so much as by how we use the capacity we own. My recommendation is that we spend the next quarter aggressively improving utilisation, defer the purchase decision by ninety days, and reserve budget for hardware only if utilisation gains stall below the threshold where they would meaningfully defer a purchase.

**Where we actually stand**

Our fleet of accelerators averages roughly forty percent utilisation, with sharp peaks around model refresh cycles and long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. That number is not unusual for teams our size, but it matters enormously when we price the alternative. A single high-memory accelerator suitable for our workloads costs on the order of a senior engineer's annual salary, before power, cooling, rack space, and the operational attention it demands. Buying hardware to serve peak demand means paying peak prices for average demand, and the gap between those two is exactly where our current waste lives.

Latency is the strongest argument for buying. Our interactive workloads do occasionally queue, and when they do, the user-visible delay is real. But the queueing data tells a more nuanced story: most latency incidents cluster in a few hours of the day and are driven by batch jobs scheduled carelessly alongside interactive traffic. If we segregate workloads properly, reserve a small slice of capacity for latency-sensitive requests, and move batch work into off-peak windows, we can likely eliminate most of the tail latency without adding a single card. That is a scheduling problem, not a supply problem.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy, and right now a single node failure during a training run costs us days. But hardware we own and underuse is its own reliability risk in disguise — it sits unpatched, unexercised, and unmonitored, so when we finally need it, it fails in ways we did not expect. Driving utilisation up forces us to build the monitoring, checkpointing, and failover discipline that improves reliability regardless of fleet size. Buying capacity first would let us postpone that work, which is precisely the wrong order of operations.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The capital we would spend on hardware is capital not spent on hiring, tooling, or the evaluation infrastructure we keep saying we need. Hardware also depreciates quickly and locks us into a power and thermal envelope that is expensive to unwind. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, are mostly software and process: better batching, quantisation where quality permits, a proper job scheduler, and honest internal charging so teams feel the cost of idle reservations. These investments are largely reversible, transferable to whatever hardware we eventually buy, and compound — a scheduler we build this quarter keeps paying off for years.

There is also a timing argument. Accelerator prices and capabilities are still moving quickly, and a purchase deferred a quarter is likely to buy more performance per dollar. Deferral is not free — we will feel some constraint, and a genuinely urgent project may be inconvenienced — but inconvenience is a cheaper currency than premature capital commitment.

**What I am uncertain about**

I want to be honest about the limits of this analysis. Our utilisation figures come from coarse instrumentation, and it is possible that a meaningful fraction of "idle" time is actually memory reserved for fast failover, which we cannot simply reclaim. If that is true, the easy wins are smaller than I estimate, and the purchase case strengthens. There is also a scenario in which demand grows faster than we expect — a successful product launch could double our inference load within weeks, and utilisation optimisation cannot conjure capacity that does not exist. That is why I am proposing we pre-approve a purchase path now, with the decision gated on end-of-quarter numbers, rather than starting the procurement conversation from scratch if we need to move fast.

**Recommendation**

Invest one quarter in utilisation: scheduling, workload segregation, measurement, and internal cost accountability. Set a concrete trigger — if peak-hour utilisation exceeds roughly seventy-five percent or latency targets are missed after optimisation — and buy then, with a clear head, knowing we exhausted the cheaper option first. The discipline this builds will make any future hardware purchase smaller, better targeted, and easier to justify.
